# Technical Brief: Instruction Scheduling and Loop Optimizations

## 1. Instruction Scheduling

### 1.1 List scheduling at the basic-block level

List scheduling is the dominant local scheduling algorithm and the substrate on which most other scheduling techniques are built. The compiler first constructs a data dependence DAG for the basic block: nodes are instructions, and edges represent true (flow) dependences, anti-dependences, output dependences, and often resource/latency annotations (an edge from producer to consumer is weighted by the issuing instruction's latency). The algorithm maintains a "ready list" of instructions whose predecessors in the DAG have already been scheduled, and at each cycle (or each slot, for a simple list scheduler without cycle simulation) it selects one or more ready instructions using a priority function, then updates the ready set by releasing successors whose dependences are now satisfied.

The classic priority heuristic is *critical path length*, computed as the node's height in the DAG, i.e., the longest latency-weighted path from that node to a DAG leaf (an instruction with no successors). Scheduling instructions with the greatest remaining critical-path distance first tends to prevent the critical path from being stalled behind non-critical work. Secondary tie-breaking heuristics include node "mobility" or slack (difference between a node's latest and earliest possible issue time), successor count (favoring instructions that unblock more future work), and register-pressure-sensitive estimates (preferring to retire live ranges). The algorithm is a greedy, polynomial-time heuristic—finding a truly optimal schedule under a general resource/latency model is NP-hard—so priority functions are engineering compromises rather than guarantees of optimality.

Correctness requires that scheduling never reorders instructions in a way that violates a dependence edge: true dependences (RAW), anti-dependences (WAR), and output dependences (WAW) must all be respected unless the compiler has first performed renaming to eliminate false (WAR/WAW) dependences. Memory dependences are handled conservatively unless alias analysis or dependence testing proves two memory accesses do not conflict; in the absence of such proof the scheduler must treat ambiguous loads/stores as ordered.

### 1.2 Trace scheduling

Trace scheduling, introduced by Fisher, extends list scheduling across basic-block boundaries to expose more instruction-level parallelism than any single block offers. The compiler uses profile information (or heuristics in its absence) to select a *trace*—a linear sequence of basic blocks along the most likely control-flow path, potentially spanning multiple branches—and schedules it as if it were a single large block, allowing instructions to move speculatively above a branch that originally preceded them, or below a branch that originally followed them, including moving instructions past the position of side-entrances and side-exits into or out of the trace.

Because instructions are moved relative to branches, the scheduler may hoist operations above a branch into a point where they execute on both the taken and the not-taken paths, or sink operations past a trace exit such that they would also need to execute off-trace to preserve correctness. This requires *compensation code*: copies of the moved instruction (or corrective fix-up instructions) inserted on off-trace edges (side entrances and side exits) so that semantics are preserved regardless of which path is actually taken at runtime. The bookkeeping for compensation code is one of trace scheduling's principal costs: it can cause code growth, and in the worst case compensation code must itself be scheduled, creating cascading bookkeeping obligations. Speculative hoisting above a branch is only sound for instructions that cannot fault problematically (or whose faults can be suppressed/deferred, e.g., via non-trapping speculative loads) and that do not have side effects observable before the branch resolves; this is the central correctness concern distinguishing trace scheduling from simple list scheduling. Because trace selection depends on predicted hot paths, mispredicted trace selection (wrong profile) can make the scheduled code suboptimal for actual runtime behavior, though it remains correct due to compensation code.

### 1.3 Software pipelining / modulo scheduling

Software pipelining overlaps successive iterations of a loop so that different pipeline stages of different iterations execute concurrently, analogous to hardware pipelining but realized by the compiler reordering and overlapping instructions in the generated code. Modulo scheduling (Rau and Glaeser) is the standard algorithmic framework: the compiler schedules a single steady-state pattern—the *kernel*—that is repeated every *initiation interval* (II) cycles, where II is the number of cycles between the start of successive loop iterations. Surrounding the kernel, the compiler generates a *prologue* that fills the pipeline (issuing the initial stages of early iterations before the first full kernel iteration completes) and an *epilogue* that drains it (completing the final stages of iterations after the last kernel execution), producing the classic prologue/kernel/epilogue structure, sometimes additionally wrapped for loop trip counts smaller than the pipeline depth.

The feasibility of a given II is checked using a *modulo reservation table* (MRT), a cyclic resource-usage table with II rows (one per congruence class modulo II); when tentatively scheduling an operation at cycle c, the scheduler checks whether the functional units/ports it needs are free at row (c mod II) and reserves them there if so, backtracking or choosing a different cycle on conflict. The *minimum initiation interval* (MII) is a lower bound on II computed as the maximum of two independently derived bounds: the *resource-constrained MII* (ResMII), which is the ceiling of (usage count of the most heavily used resource across one iteration) divided by (the number of units of that resource available per cycle); and the *recurrence-constrained MII* (RecMII), which is the maximum, over all cycles in the dependence graph (cycles arising from loop-carried dependences, i.e., cross-iteration dependence edges with nonzero distance), of (total latency around the cycle) divided by (total distance around the cycle). The scheduler attempts modulo scheduling at II = MII and, if no feasible schedule is found (due to secondary constraints like register pressure or scheduling heuristics failing within a bounded search), increments II and retries, trading throughput for feasibility.

Modulo scheduling's correctness hinges on live ranges that now span multiple, pipelined iterations: a value produced in one iteration's kernel execution may need to remain live into a subsequent iteration's kernel execution, which requires either *modulo variable expansion* (replicating a register into multiple physical registers, one per overlapping iteration, often realized with rotating register files on architectures like the Itanium) or explicit renaming via compiler-managed register rotation. Predication or explicit branch handling is required to correctly execute the ramp-up/ramp-down stages for loop trip counts that don't evenly fill the pipeline, and software pipelining trades increased code size and register pressure for improved instruction-level parallelism, making it most attractive on VLIW/EPIC and statically scheduled architectures where hardware out-of-order execution cannot recover the same overlap dynamically.

### 1.4 Pre-RA versus post-RA scheduling and the phase-ordering problem

Instruction scheduling interacts with register allocation (RA) in a way that creates a genuine phase-ordering problem, since each phase's output is most naturally the other's ideal input, yet they must be sequenced somehow. *Pre-RA scheduling* operates on virtual (unbounded) registers before allocation; it has full freedom to reorder instructions to expose parallelism and hide latency, but because it works with virtual registers, it tends to increase live-range overlap and can inflate register pressure, causing the subsequent register allocator to spill, which then inserts loads/stores that may themselves need scheduling and can invalidate the carefully constructed schedule's latency assumptions. *Post-RA scheduling* operates after physical registers are assigned; its view of true register pressure and actual physical register conflicts is accurate, but it has lost freedom because many reorderings that pre-RA scheduling could do (moving a definition far from its use) are now constrained by false dependences induced by register reuse (anti- and output dependences introduced by the allocator's choice of physical register, which may not correspond to any real serialization requirement of the program).

Common pragmatic resolutions include scheduling twice (a pre-RA pass to expose ILP and inform the allocator's live-range construction, followed by a post-RA pass to clean up stalls introduced by spill code and physical register constraints), using register-pressure-aware priority functions during pre-RA scheduling (penalizing schedules that increase the maximum simultaneously-live virtual register count, sometimes via a tracked "register pressure" metric incorporated into the priority function alongside critical-path height), or integrating scheduling and allocation more tightly (e.g., through linear scan allocators applied directly to scheduled code, or combined approaches such as integrated software pipelining with register allocation sensitivity). None of these fully eliminates the fundamental tension: there is no provably optimal ordering of the two passes in general, because the ideal schedule depends on allocation decisions and the ideal allocation depends on scheduling decisions.

### 1.5 VLIW-specific scheduling concerns and region scheduling

VLIW (very long instruction word) architectures expose multiple parallel issue slots directly in the instruction encoding and rely entirely on the compiler—there is no hardware scoreboard or out-of-order mechanism to dynamically reorder or stall—so the scheduler is solely responsible for packing independent operations into the same long instruction word while respecting all latencies, and for inserting explicit NOPs or stall cycles where no useful work is available. This makes basic-block-local list scheduling insufficient in practice, since basic blocks (especially after aggressive branching) are often too short to fill wide issue width; VLIW compilers therefore rely heavily on techniques that widen the scheduling scope beyond a single block, including trace scheduling (above) and *region scheduling*, which generalizes scheduling to an arbitrary single-entry region of the control-flow graph (not necessarily a linear trace), such as superblocks (single-entry, multiple-exit regions formed by tail duplication to eliminate side entrances) and more general DAG-shaped or hyperblock regions (predicated regions merging multiple control-flow paths into one scheduling unit using if-conversion/predication).

Region scheduling must still solve the same soundness problems as trace scheduling—speculative code motion above branches requires compensation code or non-faulting operations, and motion across region boundaries requires the region's entry/exit semantics to be preserved—but it additionally must account for VLIW-specific resource constraints: the number of issue slots per word, cross-slot functional unit restrictions (not every unit is reachable from every slot), and encoding constraints on which operation combinations can legally co-occur in one instruction word (sometimes due to immediate-field or bus-width sharing across slots). Superblock formation via tail duplication eliminates side-entrances so that intra-region code motion no longer needs compensation code for entry edges, simplifying the scheduler at the cost of code size growth from the duplicated tails. Because there is no hardware to dynamically stall on a latency miss, correctness also depends on the compiler's latency model matching the real hardware precisely—if a load's latency is mis-modeled, a dependent use scheduled too early will read stale or incorrect data with no hardware mechanism to catch the hazard.

---

## 2. Loop Optimizations

### 2.1 Loop-invariant code motion (LICM)

LICM hoists computations whose operands do not change within a loop to a point outside the loop body—typically into a *preheader*, a single-entry block inserted immediately before the loop header that dominates the loop and provides a unique insertion point—so the computation executes once instead of once per iteration. A computation is loop-invariant if all of its operands are either defined outside the loop or are themselves loop-invariant computations (a fixpoint property computed iteratively or via SSA use-def chains, where in SSA form an instruction is invariant if all reaching definitions of its operands dominate the loop). Hoisting is not valid merely because a computation is invariant; two additional correctness conditions must hold, commonly summarized under *safety* and *dominance*.

Dominance requires that the hoisted instruction's definition point (the preheader) dominate all of its original uses, which is trivially true if the instruction executed on every path through the loop originally—i.e., if the instruction dominates all loop exits (or more precisely, if it is in a block that dominates the loop's exit block), it will execute on every iteration and so hoisting it unconditionally preserves the execution count's observable effects. Safety concerns instructions that might trap or have side effects: an instruction that could raise a division-by-zero, null dereference, out-of-bounds access, or similar exception must not be executed on an iteration where the original program would not have executed it (e.g., due to a conditional block it lives in), since hoisting would speculatively execute code that the original control flow would have skipped. The standard check is whether the instruction's block dominates all exits from the loop (meaning it unconditionally executes every iteration in the original program, so hoisting introduces no new execution); if this fails, LICM requires either proving the operation cannot trap (e.g., no division by a value proven nonzero) or inserting a *speculation guard*—a runtime check replicating the original condition under which the computation was valid—before the hoisted code, falling back to the original in-loop computation otherwise. Memory operations additionally require that no other memory access in the loop may alias and modify the location being hoisted (for loads) or that the store is provably dead/redundant across iterations otherwise (for sinking stores out of a loop, the dual operation sometimes called loop-invariant store motion), which depends on alias analysis precision.

### 2.2 Strength reduction and induction variable simplification

Classical strength reduction replaces expensive operations (typically multiplications) that are driven by a loop's basic induction variable with cheaper equivalent operations (typically additions), exploiting the fact that a *linear induction variable*—one of the form i' = i + c on each iteration, or more generally a value that is an affine function of the loop trip count, j = a*i + b—can have any derived affine expression A*j + B incrementally maintained by adding a constant delta each iteration rather than recomputing the multiplication from scratch. The classical Cocke-Kennedy algorithm identifies basic induction variables (variables incremented by a loop-invariant amount each iteration, typically the loop counter) and derived induction variables (variables computed as an affine function of a basic induction variable within the loop), and for each derived induction variable of the form c1*i + c2 introduces a new variable updated by an additive increment (c1 times the basic IV's increment) each iteration, replacing the original multiplicative recomputation; this requires inserting the new variable's initialization in the preheader and its increment in the loop body, in SSA form typically appearing with a new phi-node.

The more general, SSA-based formulation is *operator strength reduction* (OSR), due to Cooper, Simpson, and Vick, which works directly on the SSA graph and generalizes beyond the basic-block-structured classical algorithm to handle arbitrary (even irreducible) control flow correctly, because it operates on the SSA def-use/use-def structure rather than requiring loop-nesting-tree-based dominance reasoning in the same way the classical algorithm does. OSR identifies "induction" regions by following chains of phi-nodes and linear recurrences (addition/subtraction of loop-invariant values, and multiplication of an induction variable by a loop-invariant value) and rewrites multiplications in terms of an accumulating addition, inserting new phi-nodes as needed; it is typically paired with *linear function test replacement*, which rewrites the loop's exit test (originally comparing the strength-reduced derived variable, now potentially eliminated, against a bound) to instead compare one of the surviving induction variables, so that strength reduction does not leave behind a now-redundant computation purely to feed the loop test. After strength reduction, a separate *induction variable elimination* pass removes induction variables that are no longer used for anything but their own increment (dead after rewriting), reducing register pressure and instruction count. Correctness requires that the replacement increment be computed from a value that is loop-invariant at the point of the derived variable's definition, and that overflow semantics are preserved; for languages or types with wraparound-defined overflow, strength reduction must replicate the exact overflow behavior of the original multiplicative computation, and for languages with undefined-behavior-on-overflow signed arithmetic, the compiler may exploit the absence of overflow to justify the transformation but must not change observable behavior when overflow does occur in ways the language disallows reasoning about.

### 2.3 Loop unrolling (full and partial) and interaction with scheduling

Loop unrolling replicates the loop body multiple times within a single iteration of a transformed loop, reducing the relative overhead of loop control (the increment, compare, and branch) per unit of useful work, and exposing more independent instructions across the replicated bodies for the scheduler to exploit. *Full unrolling* replaces the entire loop with a straight-line sequence when the trip count is a compile-time constant (or provably small), eliminating all loop control overhead and permitting further optimization such as constant propagation across what were previously separate iterations. *Partial unrolling* replicates the body a fixed unroll factor U (e.g., 4) and iterates U times fewer with a correspondingly restructured increment, requiring a *remainder loop* (or "epilogue loop," not to be confused with the modulo-scheduling epilogue) to handle trip counts not evenly divisible by U, typically generated either by peeling the remainder before or after the unrolled main loop, or by predicating/guarding the main loop's entry.

Unrolling matters for instruction scheduling because the straight-line unrolled body contains more independent operations than a single original iteration (since different unrolled copies' operations are typically mutually independent except through any loop-carried dependence), giving the scheduler a larger window across which to hide latencies and fill issue slots, which is especially valuable feeding into list scheduling or as a lightweight alternative to full software pipelining on architectures without hardware support for overlapping loop iterations. However, unrolling also increases code size (instruction cache pressure) and increases live-range overlap across the unrolled copies, which raises register pressure and can induce register allocator spilling if the unroll factor is too aggressive—mirroring the pre-RA scheduling/register pressure tension discussed earlier. Correctness of unrolling is generally straightforward for countable loops with no aliasing issues across iterations beyond what the original dependence structure already encoded, but requires care with loop-carried dependences (an unrolled copy must still respect dependences from earlier unrolled copies within the same transformed iteration) and with side effects in the remainder/peeled loop matching the original trip count exactly.

### 2.4 Loop fusion and loop fission/distribution

Loop fusion merges two (typically adjacent) loops with compatible iteration spaces into a single loop body, executing corresponding iterations together; it improves locality (data touched by both original loops in the same iteration is now accessed close together temporally, improving cache reuse) and reduces loop control overhead by amortizing it over one loop instead of two. Fusion is legal only if it does not reverse the relative order of any dependence that existed between the two original loops: formally, if loop L2 originally executed entirely after loop L1, fusion is illegal when there exists a dependence from an iteration of L2 to an earlier-or-same iteration of L1 that would, after fusion, execute out of order relative to the original program—this is typically checked via dependence testing between the two loops' array accesses and is summarized as requiring that no "fusion-preventing" dependence (a dependence whose direction would be reversed by interleaving the iteration spaces) exists. When loop bounds differ, fusion may require peeling or guarding iterations at the boundary to align the fused iteration space correctly.

Loop fission (also called loop distribution) is the inverse: it splits a single loop body into multiple separate loops, each executing a subset of the original statements over the same iteration space, which can be profitable when different parts of the loop body have conflicting resource/dependence characteristics (e.g., one part vectorizes or pipelines well and another doesn't, or splitting isolates a recurrence from the rest of the loop so that the recurrence-free portion can be optimized, parallelized, or vectorized independently) or when register pressure in the combined body is too high. Fission is legal when there is no dependence cycle spanning across the split point that would require interleaved execution of statements now assigned to different loops; dependences that only go "forward" (from the first new loop's statements to the second's) are preserved automatically by executing the loops in the corresponding order, but a dependence from the later-executing statement group back to the earlier one, if it crosses iterations such that fission would reorder it, blocks the split. Both fusion and fission rely on precise dependence analysis (direction vectors, distance vectors) between the relevant memory references.

### 2.5 Loop interchange and dependence direction vector legality

Loop interchange swaps the nesting order of two loops in a perfectly (or after transformation, imperfectly) nested loop, e.g., converting a row-major inner loop into a column-major inner loop or vice versa, primarily to improve memory locality (so that the innermost loop strides through memory contiguously matching the array's storage layout, improving spatial locality and reducing cache-line waste or enabling later vectorization along the new innermost loop) or to expose parallelism in whichever loop becomes outermost.

The legality of interchanging two loops in a nest is determined by the *dependence direction vectors* associated with every dependence between statement instances in the nest: a direction vector for a given dependence records, per loop level, whether the dependence's source and sink iterations are related by "<", "=", or ">" at that level. Interchanging loop levels i and j is legal if and only if, for every dependence in the loop nest, the direction vector does not have a forbidden pattern after the levels are swapped—concretely, interchange is illegal if swapping produces a direction vector whose leading nonzero/non-"=" entry becomes ">" where the original had the dependence correctly ordered as "<" at a now-outer level (informally: interchange must not move a "<" direction from an outer loop position to an inner one past a ">" entry, since that would reverse the apparent execution order of the dependent iterations). The standard sufficient condition taught in dependence-based frameworks is that a dependence with direction vector containing "(<, >)" (source precedes sink in the outer loop, but sink precedes source in the inner loop in the original nest) becomes illegal to interchange into "(>, <)," because that would require the sink to execute before the source, violating the dependence. Practically, compilers compute direction (and sometimes more precise distance) vectors for every pair of array references via one of several dependence tests (e.g., the GCD test as a quick necessary condition, or the Banerjee test or the Omega test for more precise linear-bound-sensitive analysis) and permit interchange only when no dependence's direction vector is violated by the reordering; the transformation is purely a permutation of loop headers and does not change the body's statements, so no compensation code is needed, but any auxiliary induction variables tied to the original nesting order must be recomputed for the new order.

### 2.6 Loop tiling/blocking for locality

Loop tiling (blocking) decomposes one or more loops of a nest into two nested loops each—an outer "tile loop" stepping by a tile size T and an inner "element loop" iterating within the tile—so that the working set touched within one execution of the tile fits within some level of the memory hierarchy (commonly the L1 or L2 cache), trading increased loop-control overhead and code complexity for dramatically improved temporal and spatial locality on data reused across the tiled dimension(s). The canonical motivating example is matrix multiplication, where tiling all three loops (over rows, columns, and the reduction dimension) with tile sizes chosen so that the working tiles of the two input matrices and the output tile simultaneously fit in cache turns an algorithm with poor cache reuse (each element reloaded many times from memory) into one with reuse confined almost entirely to cache-resident data, reducing memory bandwidth demand by a factor related to the tile size.

Tiling is legal under essentially the same dependence-direction-vector framework as loop interchange and loop skewing, because tiling is formally a combination of strip-mining (splitting one loop into two: an outer loop over tile boundaries and inner loop over elements within a tile, which is always legal since it only changes the iteration traversal grouping, not the order) followed by interchange of the resulting tile-loops and element-loops to bring tile loops outward—so tiling's legality reduces to the legality of that interchange step under the direction-vector test, meaning tiling is not always legal for arbitrary dependence patterns (for example, certain recurrences spanning the tiled dimension may forbid naive tiling without additional transformation such as skewing to make the dependence direction vectors tileable, a technique sometimes called wavefront or skewed tiling). Choosing the tile size is itself a nontrivial trade-off: larger tiles amortize loop overhead and promote reuse but risk overflowing the target cache level or causing cache or TLB conflict misses (addressed by techniques such as padding or careful tile-size selection relative to cache associativity), while smaller tiles underutilize available cache capacity; tile size selection is frequently guided by a model of the target cache's capacity and associativity or by empirical autotuning.

### 2.7 Loop-closed SSA form (LCSSA)

Loop-closed SSA form is a structural invariant maintained on top of ordinary SSA form specifically to simplify loop transformations: it requires that every SSA value defined inside a loop that has any use outside the loop be routed through a phi-node placed in the loop's exit block(s) (or more precisely, in blocks immediately dominated-by/receiving-control-from the loop exit edges), so that no use outside the loop directly references a definition from inside the loop—instead, all outside uses reference the exit-block phi, which in turn takes the in-loop value as its incoming operand along the exit edge. This single phi-node "wrapping" every loop-exiting value means that from the perspective of any transformation operating on the loop as a unit, the loop has a clean, enumerable interface of exit values, and the loop body's internal value definitions never need to be reasoned about by code outside the loop directly.

LCSSA is an enabling structure, not an optimization in itself: it simplifies loop-invariant code motion (hoisting a value out of a loop doesn't have to rewrite arbitrary downstream uses scattered through the function, since all downstream uses are mediated by the single exit phi), loop unrolling and loop unswitching (the transformation can clone or restructure the loop body and only needs to patch the operands feeding the exit phis rather than chase uses throughout the rest of the function), and inter-loop transformations like fusion and interchange (since loop-carried values crossing the loop boundary are localized to well-defined phi-nodes at the loop's structural edges, making it straightforward to verify what values flow out of a loop and update those specific edges when the loop structure changes). Maintaining LCSSA requires that after any transformation altering the loop's exit edges or body, the pass rebuilds or patches these exit phis so that the invariant continues to hold for subsequent passes; most modern loop-pass pipelines (e.g., in LLVM) enforce LCSSA as a pass precondition specifically to decouple intra-loop reasoning from whole-function SSA reasoning, trading the modest overhead of extra phi-nodes at loop exits for substantially simplified and more modular loop-transformation implementations.
